title: Prime Number
body:
An integer greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. **1 is
not prime**, and 2 is the only even one, which is the pair of edge cases every `is_prime()`
gets wrong the first time.

Trial division, using `%` from the [[Division Algorithm]]:

```c++
bool is_prime(int n) {
	if (n < 2) return false;
	for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++)
		if (n % d == 0) return false;
	return true;
}
```

Two things in there are the point of the exercise:

- **`d * d <= n`, not `d <= n`.** If `n` has a divisor above its square root, it has a
  matching one below, so there is nothing left to find past $\sqrt{n}$. This turns $O(n)$
  into $O(\sqrt{n})$, and it is most people's first taste of the argument
  [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] makes formally in [[Time Complexity]].
- **Returning early.** The moment you find one divisor you are done. A loop that sets a flag
  and keeps going gives the right answer and does needless work.

Related exercises the course actually sets: printing the first *n* primes (a
[[Counted loop]] wrapping this function), prime factorisation (divide out each factor
repeatedly), and the Sieve of Eratosthenes (an [[Array]] of [[Boolean|bool]], cross out
multiples, which trades memory for speed).

Testing this is where a [[Driver]] earns its keep, because the interesting inputs are the
boundaries: 0, 1, 2, a large prime, a perfect square.

Primes are the foundation of [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]]: RSA works because multiplying two large primes
is cheap and factoring the product is not. That gap between "easy forwards, hard backwards"
is the same one [[NP-Complete]] is about in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]. Divisibility
itself is [[DISCRETE MATH]].

## The fundamental theorem of arithmetic

**Every integer greater than 1 factors into primes, and the factorisation is unique up to the
order of the factors.** $360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$, and there is no second way to do it. That is
the reason primes are called the building blocks rather than just an interesting subset, and it is
why prime factorisation is a well-posed exercise with one right answer.

It also settles the edge case above: **if 1 counted as prime, uniqueness would fail**, since you
could staple on any number of 1s. Excluding it is bookkeeping in defence of this theorem.

Uniqueness is less obvious than existence, and it rests on Euclid's lemma (if $p \mid ab$ then
$p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$), which comes out of the extended [[Euclidean Algorithm]]. Existence is a
[[Proof By Induction|strong induction]]. Both are proved in [[DISCRETE MATH]], and
[[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] generalises the whole statement: primality becomes
[[Irreducibility]], and the same unique-factorisation theorem holds for polynomials in a
[[Polynomial Ring]].
